IRISH OFFICE  
SCOIL AN PHIARSAIGH 2025  
The annual Scoil an Phiarsaigh took place on 24th and 25th September 2025 at Ionad 
Cuimhneacháin an Phiarsaigh in Ros Muc. The event brought together close to 300 
participants including educators, students, cultural leaders, and community members to 
celebrate Padraic Pearse’s legacy and his enduring vision for the Irish language and 
education. 
The Irish Office and Customer Services team within Corporate Services, collaborated with 
our outstanding Library Services team to bring this years, new event format for this annual 
event to fruition. Both the Corporate Services team and the Library team are delighted that 
the new format has paid such dividend for all the stakeholders involved.  
Conducted entirely through Irish, this two-day programme offered a rich blend of 
discussion, performance, and creative engagement. Day one focused on “The Promise and 
Premise of Pearse,” with keynote reflections from Micheál Ó Máille on Pearse’s educational 
philosophy in today’s primary schools. Cultural highlights included traditional music by 
Comhaltas Ceoltóirí Óga Charna and Johnny Óg Connolly, storytelling by Mairín Mhic 
Lochlainn, with a circus workshop & a creative play workshop for younger attendees led by 
Stephen McGinley and Julie Anne de Brún, much to their delight. The day concluded with a 
guided tour of Pearse’s Cottage, underscoring Ros Muc’s historical and cultural significance. 
Day two explored Pearse’s radical thinking on Irish literature, art, and identity. Author Louis 
de Paor and poet Áine Ní Ghlinn led thought-provoking sessions on Pearse’s continued 
relevance in modern Ireland. Transition-year students delivered passionate talks on the 
theme “A country without a language is a country without a soul,” while Liana Glynn offered 
a student perspective on learning Irish outside the Gaeltacht. An expert panel discussed the 
viability of a bilingual Ireland, and fifth-class pupils from Gaelscoil Riada presented a creative 
film project, Mise Éire / I Am Ireland, exploring heritage and identity through a student-led 
lens.

8 
 
Scoil an Phiarsaigh remains a vital platform for cultural expression, youth engagement, and 
dialogue. It successfully blends heritage with 
creativity, reaffirming the Irish language as a 
living resource and a cornerstone of 
community and educational life.

HEALTHY IRELAND 
WOMEN’S HEALTH PROGRAMME  
 
We are now in Week 3 of the 
Empowering Women’s Health 
programme, and the response has been very positive. 
To date, 190 women have registered, with 
registration now closed for two venues—Clifden and 
Sraith Salach (Recess)—due to high demand.  
The programme has already delivered valuable and 
practical health information, including acupressure 
techniques to alleviate symptoms associated with 
perimenopause and menopause; expert insights from 
a Consultant OBGYN on managing hormonal changes; 
and holistic advice on sleep, diet, movement, and 
nutrition from an Ayurvedic practitioner and 
herbalist. 
 
This week, participants will benefit from sessions 
led by a Pelvic Floor Specialist focusing on pelvic 
health, and an HSE Health Promotion Officer with 
a physiotherapy background who will speak on 
cardiovascular and bone health. Women are 
attending in person across 15 venues throughout 
County Galway and the offshore islands, with 
talks also streamed online to ensure accessibility. 
Each session includes a Q&A session and 
concludes with an audience discussion, 
encouraging active engagement, questions, and 
reflection to support an interactive experience.

TAKING STOCK FARMER’S HEALTH PROGRAMME  
The Women in Agriculture event, led by Healthy 
County Galway in collaboration with the Irish 
Farmers' Association (IFA), saw strong attendance 
and engagement from participants in Mountbellow 
and other parts of the county.  
Held at Mountbellew Agricultural College on 1st 
October 2025, the event offered a comprehensive 
programme focused on supporting women’s 
health in agriculture and rural communities. 
Attendees availed of on-site health checks 
provided by Croí, as well as podiatry gait and foot 
diagnostic analysis by Foot Health Galway. The day 
featured a full schedule of informative talks, 
including sessions on cardiovascular health, breast cancer awareness, mental health and 
bereavement support, occupational health, and farm safety. Speakers included experts from 
Croí, the Irish Cancer Society, Embrace FARM, the Health and Safety Authority, and Teagasc. 
A panel discussion moderated by Sarah McInerney from The Farmers Journal brought 
together voices from across the sector to explore health and wellbeing among farm women.  
Information tables were available throughout the 
day from Teagasc, Healthy County Galway, IFA, 
Galway Rural Development (GRD) Leader 
Programme, the Irish Cancer Society, and 
Blueberry Hearing, ensuring attendees had access 
to a wide range of resources and supports. This 
event was a valuable addition to the Taking Stock 
programme, helping to raise awareness of the 
importance of health for women in agriculture 
and reflecting the demand for such initiatives.

COMMUNITY DEVELOPMENT AND SOCIAL INCLUSION 
CONNEMARA AND CLARINBRIDGE COMMUNITIES IN THE SPOTLIGHT FOR PRIDE 
OF PLACE AWARDS 
The Marconi Men’s Shed in Connemara and the community of Clarinbridge welcomed 
judges in mid-September from the 23rd annual IPB Pride of Place competition, an all-island 
awards programme highlighting excellence in community development. 
The judges visited the Marconi Men’s Shed in Clifden, a unique and pioneering initiative 
serving male family carers in the wider Connemara region. It is the first men’s shed in 
Ireland founded exclusively by male carers and has grown into a thriving community hub. 
Supported by FORUM Connemara CLG, the group has transformed four outbuildings into a 
well-equipped facility, combining workshop and storage areas. The shed currently has over 
50 members aged between 43 and 85, who meet regularly for a range of activities. 
Projects include a woodturning workshop, a gardening initiative in the on-site polytunnels, 
and a strong focus on health and wellbeing. Members have taken part in Tai Chi, 
mindfulness courses, healthy eating programmes, physical activity sessions, and smoking 
cessation workshops. Many participants have reported significant improvements to their 
mental and physical health, demonstrating the project’s powerful impact on quality of life.

AGE FRIENDLY PROGRAMME 
 
The Galway County Older Persons Council (OPC) received a presentation on the draft Age 
Friendly strategy for the city and county which gave members an opportunity to outline their 
observations/opinions. A number of contributions were made by members such as Housing 
grants being part of the strategy as not many people are aware of what grants there are to 
apply for. Moreover, there was a view expressed that these grants are not solely available 
online as not all older people have access to online grants or are able to apply for them online.  
It was confirmed that there is an action in the Draft Strategy in relation to inclusivity and 
digital training.  
One member stated that it would be good to see the Directory for Older People made 
available in Post Offices as that is where a lot of elderly people go to collect their pensions. 
Other members concurred and went further indicating that the Directory for Older People be 
made more widely available in places such as doctors’ surgeries and day centres.  
  
Members also received a presentation from the Age Friendly Manager for the region Dara 
McGuigan. Mr. McGuigan stated that Age Friendly Ireland doesn’t have any legal framework 
but that the functions of the Local Government are underpinned, and that Age Friendly 
Ireland works in partnership with the Local Government.  
Members were advised that enquiries would be made regarding a training workshop on age 
friendly matters.  
  
At their meeting in September new members were introduced. This meeting provided an 
opportunity for members to suggest what they would like the OPC to focus on during their

future work programme.

POSITIVE AGEING WEEK 2025 
Positive Ageing week took place at the end of September.  Positive Ageing Week is a chance 
to shine a light on the positivity of older age. The aim of the initiative is to highlight all the 
great things older people bring to our lives and communities. 
Positive Ageing Week is celebrated locally in Galway through the ‘Local Heroes Exhibition’. 
This exhibition highlights the inspiring stories of exceptional older individuals from Galway 
City and County who have graciously shared their personal experiences of ageing, 
showcasing their resilience and contributions to our community. 
The Cathaoirleach of Galway County, David Collins and the Deputy Mayor of Galway 
City, Councillor Alan Cheevers, awarded each nominee with a professional photo along with 
their biography on stage.   The exhibition was launched on the Tues 30 of September with 
an event in the Town Hall theatre, where 27 older people from Galway City and County 
were recognised and celebrated for their wonderful contribution to family, friends and 
wider society.

PUBLIC PARTICIPATION NETWORK (PPN) 
The PPN held its annual plenary meeting on September 16th in the Raheen Woods Hotel 
Athenry. 
 
The Galway County Public Participation Network (PPN) held its Plenary Meeting at Raheen 
Woods Hotel, Athenry bringing together member groups from across the county to 
network, share updates, and engage in meaningful dialogue on community development.

21 
 
From 4:00pm, over 100 attendees visited 25 exhibitor tables, hosted primarily by Galway 
County Council and a range 
of local and national 
service providers. These 
tables offered information 
on funding programmes, 
community supports, and 
public services. The 
networking session 
created a vibrant space for 
members to connect, 
share ideas, and explore 
collaboration opportunities. A short survey was given to all in attendance for future PPN 
priorities. 
The meeting officially opened by Ms. Claire Connolly PPN coordinator on behalf of PPN 
secretariat and PPN team at 5:00pm with a welcome to all invited guests, all the speakers 
and presenters, Galway County Council staff and a special welcome to all the members of 
community groups present. Mr. Patrick McHugh was introduced as master of ceremonies 
for the evening. 
Ms. Maria Heneghan gave a presentation with an overview of what the PPN is, its structures 
and its purpose. Ms Mary McGann was presented with flowers by the Secretariat for her 
many years of superb work with communities.  Mr. Michael Owens addressed all present 
about the importance of voluntary community involvement and its positive effects. 
Mr. Donal Quinn, solicitor, delivered a keynote on Wills and Estate Planning, offering 
practical advice and answering questions from attendees. His presentation was well-
received.  Ms Eimear Dolan delivered a presentation on completing grant applications and 
an overview of CSS grants, Clar & Town & Village.  Ms Tina Ryan gave a presentation on new 
funding streams for climate change projects.  Following light refreshments and finger food, a 
Q&A followed.  Questions raised were on the difficulty of using IT systems to complete grant 
applications. 
Other questions were around specific issues with Wills and inheritance which were 
answered by Mr. Donal Quinn. Ms Connolly provided detailed update on Budget, advising 
about budget for upcoming training for winter, which will be finalized in the coming weeks. 
No query arose on budget. 
The meeting concluded @8.30pm. Members were advised that the next online County 
Galway PPN Plenary will be in November.

CHARLES VALLANCEY'S IRISH GRAMMAR (1781) 
 
Galway Public Libraries’ Local Studies holds a rare 1781 edition of Charles Vallancey’s Irish 
Grammar—one of the earliest Irish language grammars published in English. Vallancey, a 
British army officer of French descent, settled in Ireland before 1760 and became deeply 
involved in antiquarian studies. He learned Irish, contributed significantly to its study, and 
helped elevate its cultural importance. A former owner of the Book of Lecan, which he 
donated to the Royal Irish Academy, Vallancey left a 
lasting legacy through his writings and dedication to 
Irish heritage. He died in 1812.

THE SUMMARY OF SOCIAL HOUSING ASSESSMENTS 2025 
The Summary of Social Housing Assessments (SSHA) is a statutory annual report compiled 
by local authorities across Ireland to determine the number of households qualified for 
social housing support whose housing needs are not currently being met. 
🔍 PURPOSE OF THE SSHA 
• It provides a point-in-time snapshot of housing need across the country. 
• Helps inform national housing policy and planning for the delivery of appropriate 
housing supports. 
• Ensures that only households with a continuing need for social housing are included. 
🏠 WHAT IS MEASURED? 
• The “net need”: total number of households qualified for social housing support but 
not currently housed through schemes like:  
o Local authority housing 
o Approved Housing Body (AHB) accommodation 
o Housing Assistance Payment (HAP) 
o Rental Accommodation Scheme (RAS) 
o Social Housing Capital Expenditure Programme (SHCEP) 
o Transfer lists 
📋 ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA 
• Households must meet income thresholds. 
• Must not already be receiving social housing support. 
• Must confirm continued need if contacted by the local authority. 
🗓️ PROCESS 
• To date Galway County Council has contacted 1,206 applicants to confirm they still 
require support, 83 applications have been closed for various reasons such changes 
to circumstance. 
• Applicants must return completed forms with updated income and household details 
by 04.11.2025.

Galway County Council’s innovative StoryMaps project, which has digitised the heritage of 
communities across County Galway into interactive online experiences, has been named a 
category winner at the 2025 Ireland eGovernment Awards. 
  
The project received the Open Data Award, having been shortlisted alongside the National 
Cancer Registry of Ireland.

133 
 
Galway County Council’s Heritage and GIS sections, working in conjunction with community 
groups and academia, have so far created over 40 town and village StoryMaps showcasing the 
rich heritage of the County’s towns, 
villages, and townlands. 
  
In addition, historical information 
relating to 1,000 townlands has been 
digitised, providing a valuable 
resource for communities, schools, 
heritage groups, Tidy Towns 
committees, academia, and the 
public.  
  
By integrating mapping technology 
with text, images, and multimedia 
content, StoryMaps delivers location-based stories that can be accessed on any internet-
enabled device, from desktop computers to tablets and phones. 
  
Cllr David Collins, Cathaoirleach of Galway County, said, “This project showcases and 
promotes knowledge of, and pride in, the rich heritage of our townlands, villages, towns, and 
other aspects of our heritage. It presents this heritage to local, national, and international 
audiences and serves as an extremely valuable resource.” 
  
Liam Conneally, Chief Executive of Galway County Council, added, “This project is a 
fantastic example of how local history can be preserved and shared using modern technology 
and innovative research techniques. The partnership approach to developing StoryMaps shows 
how collaboration is central to preserving and sharing our local history.” 
  
Liam Hanrahan, Director of Services for Planning and Economic Development, said the 
project places a strong emphasis on community engagement, presenting local heritage in a way 
that is easily accessible to the public, the Irish diaspora, and scholars at home and abroad.  
  
Led by Galway County Council’s Heritage Office and GIS Department, the project was 
developed in collaboration with the Galway County Community Archaeology Project, University 
of Galway, Atlantic Technology University (ATU) Galway, ICAN (Irish Community Archive 
Network) Galway, Galway County Heritage Forum, The Heritage Council, and local Tidy Towns, 
heritage and community groups.  
  
Bridin Feeney, GIS Analyst in Galway County Council’s ICT Department, said the project is 
about unearthing stories, local lore, and forgotten histories and presenting them in an engaging 
digital format.  
  
Outlining the background to the project, she added, “Several community groups approached us 
wanting to develop a digital platform to showcase the heritage and history of their local areas 
but lacked the capacity or resources to do so. Working with these groups, our GIS team and 
Heritage Officer developed a framework to create StoryMaps for their heritage trails and 
townland research. Some communities had the knowledge but not the digital expertise, so we

134 
 
worked with them and trained them on the possibilities of StoryMaps and how they could reach 
their target audiences.” 
  
Heritage Officer Marie Mannion said the primary goal of StoryMaps is to make heritage 
accessible to everyone. 
  
“We initially expected to train local communities and students on how to create StoryMaps and 
make this information available as open-source data. It has turned out to be much more than 
that,” she explained. “It has given people confidence in their skills and fostered a strong sense 
of pride in their communities. The StoryMaps are used by local residents, schools, academics, 
the diaspora, and many others. They have a myriad of uses, and we are only now discovering 
additional applications, including their use in ATU Galway’s Heritage Studies course.” 
  
The Ireland eGovernment Awards celebrate excellence, innovation, and creativity in Ireland’s public 
sector and are recognised as the benchmark for digital government services. This year’s awards 
were presented by An Taoiseach Micheál Martin TD at O’Reilly Hall, UCD. 
  
Giles Newsome, CEO of iConnect101 and a member of this year’s judging panel, said, “This 
submission proved very much the value of using 
GIS, open-source mapping data to deliver 
something very valuable from Galway County 
Council to the people of Galway and beyond. 
What has been done here is the creation and 
curation of very valuable content on interactive 
maps about places of interest, historic 
monuments, historic sites right across County 
Galway. A fantastic smart use of mapping 
technology.”

INVASIVE SPECIES ERADICATION – WEST CONNACHT ISLANDS 
The Invasive Species Eradication Programme on the West Connacht Islands is a joint 
initiative between the Biodiversity Offices of Mayo and Galway County Councils and the 
ACRES West Connacht Cooperation Project (CP). It focuses on Inishbofin in County Galway, 
and Inishturk and Clare Island in County Mayo. Community outreach is taking place through 
horticulture and invasive species identification workshops for residents and landowners,

135 
 
alongside botanical surveys to identifying and mapping invasive plant species, the creation 
of tailored Invasive Species Management Plans for each 
island, and the application of treatment measures. This 
multi-faceted approach ensures that both ecological and 
social dimensions of invasive species management are 
addressed—building local capacity, improving awareness, 
and enabling long-term, site-specific solutions that are 
informed by scientific data and community input.  
Invasive Alien Plant Species are a significant threat to 
biodiversity. Invasive species can cause the decline in native 
species through competition for light, space and food 
sources. Invasives such a rhododendron or giant rhubarb 
often creates dense stands of growth if left unchecked or 
unmanaged, this over time can impact badly upon the 
landscape. 
The Invasive Species Eradication Programme on West Connacht Islands is unique in the 
advantage of the geographical locations of the islands and the natural barriers to invasive 
species spread i.e. distance from mainland and the barrier of the Atlantic Sea. This provides 
immense opportunity to use the natural advantage of the island’s location in the prevention 
of invasive species spread and the development of targeted eradication plans.

Storm Amy, the 1st storm of the 2026/2026 season hit on Friday 3rd October with an Orange 
Wind warning in effect from 2pm until 10pm. It was preceded by a Yellow warning for 
rainfall on the 2nd October, which lasted most of the day, and again returned on the morning

Secondary N59 road did not escape, and it was closed at a location east of Clifden near Pine 
Island Viewing Point and also near Kylemore Abbey and Lake. Temporary Traffic lights were

deemed too unsafe to leave them in situ after darkness, so the decision was made to close

services. 
 
In Maigh Cuilinn, Conamara South Council staff, aided by local contractors managed to re-
open the ‘Mountain Road’ near the Playground the evening of the 2nd October and kept it

Roads issues during evenings, at night and at weekends. Over the weekend there were 
multiple outdoor staff ‘on call’ together with attendant crews, plant and equipment.  
During this event, as with all severe weather events, the Council maintained 
communications with the crews on the ground, the Fire Service, the Civil Defence and An 
Garda Siochana. The Council benefited from its’ bespoke self-developed management IT 
system for such events called ‘SWEMS’ (Severe Weather Emergency Management System). 
This enables us to map incidents and damage as we become aware of same to facilitate a 
clear picture of storm impact and the targeting of our resources.
